claim: Eta-squared is a positively biased estimator of the population effect size, with the bias remaining considerably large even at n=100 per group.
stance_target: Mandatory Fix 9: eta-squared is positively biased at small n
scope_conditions: One-way fixed-effect ANOVA with independent samples; Monte Carlo simulation with 1,000,000 replications per condition across six population-effect-size x variability conditions, n=10 to 100 per group
quoted_support: "eta2 has a considerable large positive bias, even when sample size is 100." "Note that for all three effect size indices, the absolute bias becomes larger when the sample size is small."

claim: Epsilon-squared and omega-squared are inferential, bias-corrected effect size indices constructed by substituting bias-corrected sample estimators for the variance component parameters that eta-squared estimates naively.
stance_target: Mandatory Fix 9: omega-squared/epsilon-squared as bias-corrected alternatives to eta-squared
quoted_support: "eta2 was developed as a descriptive index while epsilon2 and omega2 were intended for inferential purposes ... epsilon2 and omega2 are inferential indices which correct the bias in estimating the population effect size, eta2. Both epsilon2 and omega2 are constructed by substituting the variance component parameters of eta2 with its bias-corrected sample estimators."

claim: Contrary to the decades-old common belief that omega-squared is the least biased of the three indices, Okada's Monte Carlo study finds epsilon-squared has the least absolute bias in every sampled condition, with omega-squared's negative bias always larger in magnitude than epsilon-squared's.
stance_target: Mandatory Fix 9's characterization of which correction is 'the' bias-corrected alternative
scope_conditions: One-way ANOVA, six simulated population-effect-size x variability conditions, n=10-100/group
quoted_support: "epsilon2 has the least absolute bias among the three indices, surpassing omega2 in all the conditions, in contrast with the commonly-held belief that omega2 is less biased than epsilon2 (Grissom & Kim, 2004; D. Matsumoto, et al., 2011)."

claim: Eta-squared's bias, while smallest in standard deviation among the three indices (making it 'efficient' in Keselman's 1975 terms), is nonetheless large enough in magnitude at small n that standard deviation alone is an insufficient quality criterion; RMSE is needed.
quoted_support: "it is important to remember that eta2 has a considerably large bias when the sample size is small, and that an estimator would have a small standard deviation even if its estimates were consistently off deviate from the true value. It is therefore insufficient to determine the quality of an estimator based only on its standard deviation."

claim: None of the three sample effect-size estimators (eta-squared, epsilon-squared, omega-squared) is an unbiased estimator of the population effect size parameter, though all three converge to the same value as sample size tends to infinity.
stance_target: Precision of the bias-correction claim (correction reduces but does not eliminate bias)
quoted_support: "it is shown that none of the three sample effect size measures (eta2, epsilon2, and omega2 ...) is an unbiased estimator of eta2 (Darlington, 1968). It is also shown that as sample size tends to infinity, eta2, epsilon2, and omega2 all converge toward the same value (Maxwell et al, 1981)."
